title: Ants! Part 2!
summary: Part two of a two-part Stuff You Should Know series on ants. Chuck opens with a note that the SketchFest live show in San Francisco has been postponed due to Omicron. The hosts cover ant social structure: queens versus worker ants, lifespans, male ants and their short lives, and how colonies are organized with major and minor workers. They discuss a giant underground nest excavated after being filled with concrete, and the concept of force chains that load-bearing grains of soil form. They cover army ants' nomadic bivouacs, Argentine ant super colonies spanning Italy to Spain, and how ants spread via ship ballast. They discuss nuptial flights, when winged virgin queens and males mate and new colonies form, and leafcutter ants farming fungus. Communication via pheromones, stigmergy, and touch is covered, along with a computer model of nest building and ant burial and nursing behavior. The episode closes with a listener suggestion from Joey in Tucson and sign-off.
topics: Stuff You Should Know ants part 2

segments.title: Opening note and intro
segments.summary: Chuck announces SketchFest in San Francisco is postponed due to Omicron, then Josh and Chuck introduce part two on ants.

segments.title: Social insects and the ant queen
segments.summary: The hosts describe social insects, the single queen who lays eggs, and how queens differ from worker ants mainly in size and having functional ovaries. Queens can live up to thirty years while workers live about a year.

segments.title: Male ants and worker roles
segments.summary: Male ants hatch from unfertilized eggs, live about a week, and exist to mate with the queen. Workers do nearly all the colony work, including feeding, defense, and care for young. Major and minor workers can specialize.

segments.title: Ant sex determination and colony survival
segments.summary: The hosts explain that males come from unfertilized eggs and the queen fertilizes some eggs to make workers. Some species' workers can lay unfertilized eggs to produce males if the queen dies. A brief tangent about moles and a Pipe Piper episode follows.

segments.title: Underground nests and force chains
segments.summary: A concrete-cast excavated nest, about the size of a Little League field and twenty-six feet deep, showed efficient tunnel design. Ants dig at the angle of repose and keep load-bearing grains of soil in force chains, which they seem to be coded to do.

segments.title: Army ants, nomadism and super colonies
segments.summary: Army ants are nomadic and make temporary bivouacs of their own bodies. Argentine ants form a super colony stretching about 3,700 miles from Italy to Spain in Europe, unlike their genetically diverse home in Argentina. Humans spread ants via ship ballast.

segments.title: Nuptial flights and leafcutter ant farming
segments.summary: When colonies get too big, winged virgin queens and males fly off in nuptial flights and mate in the air. New queens found colonies alone. Leafcutter ants cut leaves to grow fungus they farm, which feeds their young and produces antibiotics.

segments.title: Pheromones and ant communication
segments.summary: Ants communicate mainly through pheromones, with alarm signals, recruitment, food trails, and the stigmergy concept. They also use touch, drumming, and stridulation. Pheromones dissipate so trails fade when food runs out.

segments.title: Nest building model, burial and nursing
segments.summary: A computer model following three simple rules produced realistic nest chambers and tunnels. Ants keep cemeteries, and some species carry injured ants home to be nursed with antibiotics.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention listener Joey from Tucson for suggesting the ants topic, give the contact email, and sign off.
